Documentation
Documentation that means the work does not stop when the key person leaves: knowledge and the reasons behind decisions are on paper, and one named person is responsible for keeping it current.
Problem

When technical knowledge and the reasons behind important decisions live only in one person's head, that person leaving means the work stops. And documentation that exists but has no owner for updates stops being trustworthy after a few changes.

And when there is no document and something breaks, everyone blames someone else. We have seen a client stuck between several contractors where nobody would take responsibility, because nothing had been written down at the start.

We build documentation like a product: first we audit what exists, what is missing, and what is wrong, then we assign each document an audience, a format, an update rule, and an owner, and we hand it over reviewed by your own team. We also do not write documentation without a source, because documentation without a source is a guess. We have also published the scope template we sign before every project, so you can see what a good document looks like: dadmor’s real project scope template.
Who it is for

items: Teams with a product or API that customers or outside developers must use without asking you.
Businesses moving a project from one team or contractor to another.
Teams that want to know why a technical decision was made, not only what was decided.

blocks.html: Who it is not for

items: If you want a document that sits in a folder and nobody reads.
If access to the system, the code, or the people who know it is not possible. Documentation without a source is guesswork.
If you need legal text (contracts, terms of use, a formal privacy policy); that is a lawyer's job.

blocks.html: Artefacts we write
Approach

items: Audit. Input: existing documents, system access, and conversations with key people. Output: a list of what exists, what is missing, and what is wrong. Owner: dadmor.
Structure. Input: the audit. Output: a document list with audience, format, update rule and owner for each. Owner: dadmor; approval: you.
Write. Input: approved structure and access to sources. Output: the documents, reviewed by one person on your team. Owner: dadmor; technical review: you.
Handover. Input: approved documents. Output: documents in their final location, with a session showing how to keep them updated. Owner: dadmor.

blocks.html: Scope and timeline factors

items: What changes the size of the work: number of documents, number of API endpoints, bilingual output, and how available the sources (code, people) are.
What you supply: system and code access, key people's time, and one technical reviewer.
What delays projects: a key person with no time to talk, and a system that changes while it is being documented.

blocks.html: Effort band

items: A separate fixed proposal for each phase. The audit can be ordered on its own.

blocks.html: This band is a starting estimate and depends on the current state of your documents; it is settled after the scoping conversation, once we have seen them.
Limits and risks

items: A document stays correct only while its update rule is followed. After handover, that is the job of the owner named in the structure.
We do not write legal text.
We publish a sample of your documents only with your permission, and redacted.
